item.title: Deep transformer-enhanced dynamic structured light for three-dimensional moving object imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) projects a sequence of sinusoidal fringe patterns, each shifted by a known amount, and recovers the 3D shape of a surface from the phase of the captured images. It is robust to ambient light and to changes in surface reflectivity, but it needs at least three images, and the object must stay still while they are taken. If the object moves, each surface point is lit by different projector pixels and seen by different camera pixels in each frame, so the phase steps between frames are no longer the intended ones. The result is ripples, phase-unwrapping errors or a failed reconstruction.

Faster projectors and cameras reduce the problem but raise hardware cost, and the effect of motion still remains. Most error-estimation methods handle motion only along the depth direction and do not address the pixel mismatch caused by motion in other directions. Tracking-based compensation models such as Lu’s work well within the X–Y plane but handle Z-direction motion poorly, and methods that estimate a single global translation miss local, pixel-level motion differences. When an object moves in an arbitrary direction, every surface point has its own displacement and therefore its own phase error.

How it works

The method keeps standard four-step phase shifting and adds two things: a learned tracker that finds where each pixel of one fringe image went in the next ones, and a pixel-wise model of the phase error that remains after that tracking. Both run inside a short sliding window of five frames.

  1. Model the motion-induced phase error. The projector cycles four-step fringes (π/2 apart) while the camera captures the moving object. The motion of each surface point is split into an in-plane displacement, which moves the point to another pixel (Δu, Δv), and a displacement along Z, which adds a phase error. The total phase error is the sum of the two.
  2. Track pixels with a transformer. The image sequence is split into windows of five frames, and the middle frame is the key frame. A COTR (COrrespondence TRansformer) network, initialised with its original pre-trained weights and fine-tuned on fringe images, matches query pixels in the key frame to the other four frames. A shared CNN backbone extracts features from both images, a transformer encoder–decoder relates them, and an MLP head predicts each match.
  3. Align the frames and solve for the Z error. The matches define a pixel-wise mapping that aligns all five frames so the same surface point is followed through the window. Within the short window, the Z-direction velocity is treated as constant, so each frame adds the same extra phase error ε, and frame n of the window (n = 1 to 5, key frame n = 3) carries a Z part of (n − 3)ε. Combining the intensities of the five frames gives three equations in the object phase Φ and ε. For small ε they reduce to a linear equation K1ε + K0 = 0, which is solved at every pixel, and the corrected phase Φ follows.
  4. Unwrap and reconstruct. The corrected wrapped phase is unwrapped with a three-frequency phase-shifting algorithm, using two sets of lower-frequency fringes projected alternately with the high-frequency ones, and converted into 3D shape with the calibrated camera–projector model.
  5. Slide the window. The window moves on by one frame, so each newly acquired image, together with the four before it, gives a new 3D shape of the object.

Results

RMSE 0.072 mm on a moving ceramic plate, against 1.401 mm for standard PSP and 1.352–2.028 mm for Guo’s, Lu’s and Wang’s methods (Section 3.2, Fig. 6).
RMSE 0.096 mm on a moving “Aphrodite” statue, against 1.129 mm for PSP (Section 3.3, Fig. 8).
Fringe-image matching error (AEPE) 0.47–0.83 px for the fine-tuned COTR, against 12.32–21.06 px for optical flow on five unseen objects (Table 1).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.092 mm with COTR as the tracker, against 0.157, 0.181 and 0.490 mm with fine-tuned FlowFormer, GMFlow and RAFT in a combined-motion experiment (Table 2).

The system uses a high-speed camera at 512 × 512 pixels and 30 fps and a DLP projector. To fine-tune COTR, the authors captured 45 dynamic scenes of sculptures, toys and industrial parts on a shallow box of sand (about 5 cm deep), with 60 motions each, giving 2,700 pairs of pre- and post-motion fringe images (2,400 for training, 300 for validation). Ground-truth matches came from an extra blank image projected at each pose, on which a robust local optical flow method computed dense displacements. Training converged after about 1,400 epochs and took about 42 hours.

The ceramic plate was moved by a translation stage at 40° to the camera’s optical axis in 1 mm steps, with a 12-step phase-shifting measurement as ground truth. Standard PSP shows clear ripple distortion. Guo’s method smooths part of it, Lu’s method compensates only motion in the X–Y plane, and Wang’s method simplifies the phase-shift error, which leads to even larger errors. With steps of ±1, ±2 and ±3 mm, the RMS error of the proposed method stays below 0.1 mm (Fig. 6(f)). On the statue, PSP shows stripe artifacts and discontinuities along the edges, Guo’s method still has large errors at the edges, and Lu’s method leaves periodic ripples because Z-direction motion is not compensated; the proposed method recovers the contour more accurately.

The method was also tested on a static statue next to a rotating one, on a rotating fan model with a smooth, weakly textured surface, on a statue on a continuously rotating platform, and on objects that translate and rotate at the same time. Under combined translation and rotation, the rotation adds phase deviations of up to about 1 rad in the outer regions, and the method still keeps most surface areas accurate. The authors note its limits: when the translation along Z is too large, phase-error estimation can still fail (marked regions in Fig. 12); the authors suggest increasing the projection rate or combining the framework with geometry-constraint-based or Gray-code-based unwrapping. Because the estimate relies on a five-frame window, the method works reliably for small inter-frame motion; standard frame rates suffice for slow to moderate motion, while fast objects need high-frame-rate cameras and projectors.

item.title: VeinTr: Robust end-to-end full-hand vein identification with transformer
item.description:
The problem

Hand vein identification recognises a person from the vein pattern of the hand, imaged under near-infrared light. Typical systems follow four steps: locate the hand, extract a region of interest (ROI), extract features from it, and match the result against a database of enrolled hands. Earlier work built hand-crafted geometric or statistical descriptors, which suffer under perturbations such as illumination changes and noise; more recent methods learn the features with convolutional neural networks.

Even the learned methods still work on an ROI, usually cut from the palm. That brings two drawbacks. The preprocessing is complex, and accuracy depends on how robustly the ROI is extracted, which is hard in real applications. And the crop throws information away: the vein pattern across the whole hand is unique to each person, so a representation built from only part of it is potentially inferior to one that uses the full pattern.

How it works

VeinTr skips ROI extraction and takes the full-hand image directly as input. Its identification has only two steps, feature extraction and probe-to-database matching. The feature extractor combines a convolutional local feature encoder, a lightweight transformer and an MLP-based global feature decoder, and the whole network is trained end to end as a metric-learning task.

  1. No ROI crop. Conventional pipelines locate the hand and crop a palm ROI before extracting features, so veins outside the crop are lost. VeinTr feeds in the whole hand image instead.
  2. Local features. Convolution blocks (convolution, batch normalisation, PReLU) reduce the size of the 256×256 input while extracting local features, and three residual blocks refine them into a 64×64×64 local feature map.
  3. Global aggregation with attention. The feature map is cut into 16 patches of 16×16, which are flattened and projected to a lower dimension. Three multi-head attention layers with 8 heads relate every patch to every other one, enlarging the receptive field from local to the whole hand.
  4. One feature per hand. The global feature decoder flattens the attention output and applies a two-layer MLP with batch normalisation, giving a 512-dimensional hand vein feature. Training uses the ArcFace loss, which pulls features of the same hand together and pushes different hands apart.
  5. Probe-to-database matching. The normalised features of the enrolled hands form a database matrix D. A probe hand is assigned to the identity C with the highest similarity score, C = argmax(D · ‖VeinTr(p)‖), where ‖·‖ denotes normalisation.

Results

Correct recognition rate 99.85 % at 850 nm and 99.92 % at 940 nm on CASIA, the highest in the paper’s comparison with six hand-crafted and six deep-learning methods (Table 1).
Equal error rate 0.10 % and 0.09 % (the point where false accepts equal false rejects), against 0.51 % for the best hand-crafted method (NMRT) and 3.71 % for PVSNet (Table 1).
Trained on CASIA, 98.17 % on TPV and 97.62 % on PLUSVein without retraining (Table 2).

All methods in the comparison work on a palm or finger ROI; VeinTr is the only one that uses the full hand. On CASIA, all hand-crafted methods already exceed 90 % correct recognition and the earlier method NAF is close to saturation at 99.83 % and 99.50 %, so VeinTr’s lead in recognition rate is small (0.02 and 0.42 points); in equal error rate it is 0.41 points below NMRT and 3.61 below PVSNet (Table 1). For inter-dataset tests, VeinTr is trained on one dataset and tested on all three. Models trained on CASIA or TPV stay above 90 % correct recognition on every test set. PLUSVein is much smaller (420 images of 42 volunteers), and the model trained on it generalises less well, reaching 89.76 % on CASIA and 81.43 % on TPV.

The ablation study (all models trained on CASIA) shows that both parts of the network matter. Without the attention layers, the correct recognition rate drops to 83.43 % on CASIA, 65.14 % on TPV and 55.10 % on PLUSVein; without the residual blocks, it drops to 95.12 %, 75.07 % and 83.67 % (Table 3). With three attention layers the rate saturates on CASIA and peaks on TPV and PLUSVein; a fourth and fifth layer lower it, which the authors attribute to overfitting. Three residual blocks are chosen as a trade-off between recognition rate and computational cost. As future work, the authors plan to fuse full-hand vein information with full-hand print data.

item.title: TopFormer: Topology-Aware Transformer for Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration estimates the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping scans. Most learned methods describe each point by its local geometry, match the descriptors, reject outliers with RANSAC and solve for the transformation. Recent Transformer-based methods work on a sparse, sub-sampled set of points and let every sparse point attend to all the others, and some add the points’ relative positions so that attention knows where each point sits.

Sub-sampling throws away fine-grained structure, though, and relative position does not help when two sparse points are close to each other in space but far apart along the surface. The paper’s example is the top of a chair next to the corner of a desk: the two points have similar local geometry because they lie in the same neighbourhood, and their relative position barely separates them because they are close in Cartesian space. Their features become ambiguous and lead to wrong matches. In the dense point cloud the difference is easy to see, since the route from one to the other along the surface is long; in the sparse points it is hard to observe.

How it works

TopFormer follows a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline and adds one ingredient: a topological structure encoding that tells the Transformer how each pair of sparse points is connected along the surface. Because the sparse points are a subset of the dense points, this surface information can be measured on the dense cloud and handed to the sparse points, which the authors call a sparse-through-dense strategy.

  1. Close in space, far along the surface. A KPConv encoder extracts local features at a sparse and a dense level. Two sparse points such as a chair top and a desk corner can look alike to it, and their relative position does little to separate them.
  2. Sparse points inside the dense graph. Down-sampling uses furthest point sampling, so every sparse point is also a dense point. On the dense points, TopFormer builds a K-nearest-neighbour graph, keeping only edges shorter than a radius τ.
  3. Geodesic distance by shortest path. For two sparse points p and q, Dijkstra’s algorithm on the dense graph gives the geodesic distance from p to q, the length of the shortest route along the surface.
  4. Direction from normals, independent of their sign. Normals estimated by PCA are unoriented, and scans can be in arbitrary poses, so the normals are hard to re-orient consistently. TopFormer therefore uses the sines of the angle between the normal at p and the vector from p to q, and of the angle between the two normals; flipping a normal turns an angle α into π − α and leaves the sine unchanged.
  5. Encoding inside attention, then matching. The geodesic distance, the Euclidean distance and the two sines are mapped by a sinusoidal function into the topological structure encoding, which is added to the keys of self-attention. Cross-attention then lets the two clouds exchange information; sparse points are matched from a confidence matrix, the matches are refined at the dense level with an optimal transport layer, and RANSAC estimates the final rotation and translation.

Results

Registration recall (share of scan pairs aligned to an RMSE below 0.2 m) of 92.4 % on 3DMatch and 75.1 % on 3DLoMatch with 5,000 correspondences, against 92.0 % and 75.0 % for GeoTransformer (Table 1).
On KITTI, 99.8 % registration recall with a relative translation error of 6.7 cm, the lowest in the comparison (Table 2).
Removing the topological structure encoding lowers recall to 89.7 % and 67.4 % on 3DMatch and 3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The indoor experiments use 3DMatch and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch, which holds the scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m, computed with 50K RANSAC iterations. TopFormer’s registration recall is the highest, or tied for highest, at every correspondence number tested (5,000 down to 250) on both splits, and its feature matching recall on 3DMatch stays between 98.4 % and 98.7 %.

Its inlier ratio is below GeoTransformer’s at 5,000 correspondences (71.7 % against 71.9 % on 3DMatch, 37.2 % against 43.5 % on 3DLoMatch), but higher at smaller numbers, for example 82.8 % against 76.0 % on 3DMatch and 53.1 % against 46.2 % on 3DLoMatch at 1,000. On the outdoor KITTI odometry data, most of the compared methods already reach 99.8 % recall; TopFormer matches that, with a rotation error of 0.27°.

The ablation study shows that both parts of the encoding contribute. Without the geodesic distance, registration recall falls from 92.4 % to 90.3 % on 3DMatch and from 75.1 % to 72.3 % on 3DLoMatch; without the normal-based directional terms it falls to 91.9 % and 73.9 %. Dropping the encoding entirely, which leaves a vanilla Transformer, costs 2.7 and 7.7 points of recall, and the inlier ratio falls by 8.6 and 5.6 points.
